headline_marked: IRGC Claims [[Amazon's Bahrain Data Center Destroyed]] by Cruise Missiles in Retaliation
headline: IRGC Claims Amazon's Bahrain Data Center Destroyed by Cruise Missiles in Retaliation
summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps claims to have struck an AWS data center in Bahrain with cruise missiles on July 21, unconfirmed by Amazon or CENTCOM, in retaliation for a US strike on an Iranian nuclear plant.
details: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on July 21 that its Aerospace Force struck and destroyed Amazon Web Services’ (AWS) data center in Bahrain using several cruise missiles. This alleged attack was stated as retaliation for a US strike on Iran’s Darkhovin nuclear power plant two days prior. The claim remains unconfirmed by Amazon or CENTCOM.

If true, this would mark the first reported use of cruise missiles against commercial cloud infrastructure in the Gulf conflict. The IRGC also claimed hits on US air-defense radar at Muharraq and a Patriot battery at Riffa in Bahrain as part of the same operation. This suggests the IRGC views commercial cloud facilities as militarily equivalent targets.

The IRGC's public relations office, through Mehr News Agency and Tasnim, stated the attack was "in continuation of the 24th wave of Operation Nasr-2." It explicitly linked the strike to "aggression and violation by the child-killing American army against the under-construction and civilian facilities at Darkhovin."

The coordinated nature of the alleged strikes, targeting both air-defense installations and a commercial data center, indicates a deliberate operational planning. This approach treats a data center as a military-grade objective, warranting the same strategic consideration as radar and interceptor batteries.

No strike imagery was provided by the IRGC to substantiate the claim. This marks the first time the Guard has explicitly linked a commercial infrastructure strike to a nuclear facility, even one under construction.

The US attack on Iran’s Darkhovin nuclear power plant, which Iran's Atomic Energy Organization confirmed occurred on July 19, 2026, was confirmed by CENTCOM as part of strikes on Iranian military infrastructure. The IRGC's claim regarding AWS came approximately 48 hours after the Darkhovin strike.

Darkhovin is a 360-megawatt nuclear power plant under construction in Khuzestan province, with no nuclear material on site at the time of the US strike. Iran's AEOI condemned the US attack as a violation of international law, and Iran's UN Ambassador demanded Security Council condemnation.

This retaliation framing establishes a new escalation tier within Operation Nasr-2. The IRGC's previous waves targeted military objectives, but Wave 24's explicit linkage to a nuclear facility suggests any US strike on Iranian nuclear infrastructure could authorize retaliatory strikes on US commercial infrastructure in the Gulf.

headline_marked: [[Hanwha security camera firmware shipped GitHub admin token]] with access to hundreds of repositories
headline: Hanwha security camera firmware shipped GitHub admin token with access to hundreds of repositories
summary: A security researcher discovered a hardcoded GitHub admin token in Hanwha Vision camera firmware, granting full access to hundreds of the company's private repositories.
details: A security researcher analyzing Hanwha Vision security camera firmware discovered a hardcoded GitHub admin token. This token was duplicated across approximately 30 files within the firmware image.

The token provided administrative privileges to hundreds of repositories within Hanwha's GitHub organization. This level of access could allow an attacker to view, modify, or delete code, potentially introducing further vulnerabilities.

The root cause appears to be a misconfiguration during the build process. The camera's UI, built with Vite, was set to include the entire process.env at build time, inadvertently embedding the CI job's environment variables, including the GitHub token, into the firmware.

While it's unclear if the token was actively served to users accessing the camera's admin UI, it resided on disk within the firmware. The researcher noted this isn't the first instance of an organization shipping GitHub tokens in firmware.

Further analysis of environment variables within the firmware revealed IP addresses assigned to the US Department of Defense. Hanwha Vision, formerly Samsung Techwin, is a subsidiary of Hanwha Group, which also manufactures military hardware like the K9 Thunder artillery and SGR-A1 sentry robots.
